title: I made a roguelike deckbuilder where you and the enemy share one deck. Art, music and code are all AI-assisted, and it’s playable in the browser.
author: oxygenal
selftext:
Littlewell and Below is a cozy roguelike deckbuilder with one twist: you and each critter draw from the same deck, the Well, and fight over who owns every card. Mark a card to make it yours, Stack it on top for your next draw, or Sink it out of reach. A card you play can end up in the enemy’s hand next turn.

Play it free in your browser: [https://oxygenal.itch.io/littlewell-and-below](https://oxygenal.itch.io/littlewell-and-below)

How it was made. Most of it is AI-generated on a local ComfyUI, with a lot of picking and fixing:

Critters: Z-Image stills. Qwen-Image-Edit outpainted any critter that was cut off at the frame’s edge. 

Cards: one painted icon per card, 314 in all. Prompting for “card icon” kept drawing little cards with labels on them, so the prompts ask for single objects instead.

Backdrops: layered paintings drawn in WebGL with parallax, wind and light. A depth map of each painting decides which parts sway, so leaves move and walls don’t.

Music: Stable Audio 3, about 2,000 takes for 12 loops. SongEval ranked them, and a separate repetition check threw out catchy takes that loop the same two bars forever. SongEval alone liked those.

Code: TypeScript, written with Claude Code. The rules engine is deterministic, and bots play millions of simulated fights to balance it. I didn’t trust my own playtests for the numbers.

It’s still in development, so I’d love feedback on the game itself.

comments.author: Crunchfest3
comments.body: I'd be curious what your simulations show about the worst Stack/Mark loops. How long can one side keep deciding what the other gets to draw, and what actually breaks that control? A matchup could have an even win rate while being miserable for whoever falls behind first. Saving replays of the longest stretches without a useful response might reveal more than average damage or win rate. With a shared deck, being allowed back into the fight seems like a balance question of its own.

replies.author: oxygenal
replies.body: That’s a sharp question, and our existing numbers can’t answer it. I’ll build a measurement for it

replies.author: oxygenal
replies.body:
I had the game’s AI play itself 2,000 times in evenly matched fights, and tracked two things:

\- **How often your draw was rigged by your opponent**: about 1 turn in 5.

\- **How often a rigged draw left you with nothing useful to do** (no damage, no defence, no way to fight back): about 1 turn in 100. It never happened more than 2 turns in a row. In about a quarter of the cases the player who got rigged simply rearranged the deck back.

On getting back into the fight: whoever falls clearly behind first still wins about 28% of the time. I reran it with all the rigging and claiming cards banned, and comebacks came out the same, about 28%. So the deck control doesn’t seem to lock people out more than a normal race does.

I’m also keeping replays of the worst stretches, as you suggested, and one enemy does stand out, so I’m watching that matchup. These are AI players, so humans might still find nastier tricks.
